title: Syllabus
text:
Course description
Experiments are one of the main ways in which we expand our understanding of biology. In this hands-on course, students will develop fundamental skills in experimental design, data analysis, and visualization. Students will also learn how to use the coding language R to analyze and visualize data. By the end of the course, students will be able to describe experimental designs and analytic techniques (t-tests, ANOVA, linear regression, mixed effects models, etc.) commonly used in biological research. Students will also be able to evaluate the appropriateness of different experimental designs in biological research, design experiments to answer specific questions, and work through analytic workflows of medium complexity.
The course runs in three modules — see the full Schedule for week-by-week topics:

R Crash Course (Weeks 1–3) — introduction to R, data management best practices, and the typical analytic workflow for experimental work in the life sciences.
Data Exploration (Weeks 4–6) — working with data in R, focused on summarizing and visualizing key characteristics of biological data.
Statistical Analysis and Interpretation (Weeks 7–14) — commonly used experimental designs and the statistical techniques typically used to analyze biological data, pairing fundamental principles with applied practice each week. After Spring Break (Weeks 9–14) the module is organized around the idea that common statistical tests are linear models: t-tests, ANOVA, ANCOVA, correlation, chi-square tests, and (with extensions) mixed-effects models are all special cases of one framework. We interpret every model with the marginaleffects R package, which turns fitted models into predictions, comparisons, and slopes in the units of the data.

title: Syllabus
text:
Learning objectives
At the end of this course, students will be able to:

Apply principles of data management and project organization to facilitate the analysis of experimental data.
Use the R coding language to import, clean, analyze, and visualize experimental data.
Produce robust exploratory data analyses and visualizations for commonly encountered experimental designs.
Discuss the appropriateness of different statistical tests for various experimental designs.
Explain how common statistical tests (t-tests, ANOVA, correlation, chi-square) are special cases of the linear model, and fit them as such in R.
Extend linear models to multiple predictors, interactions, non-normal responses (GLMs), and non-independent data (mixed-effects models).
Interpret model results as estimates with uncertainty using marginal effects (predictions, comparisons, and slopes) rather than p-values alone.
Interpret the results of key statistical analyses.

Required course materials
The primary requirement is access to Canvas and a UML email account. This course will also require R for Data Science, version 2, by Wickham, Çetinkaya-Rundel, and Grolemund. You’re welcome to purchase a hard copy, but the text is also freely available online. We will also use free R packages including the tidyverse, marginaleffects, and lme4 (installation instructions are in the first tutorials); the marginaleffects book is freely available online and Lindeløv’s “Common statistical tests are linear models” is a recommended supplement. Attendance, engagement, and classroom etiquette
Attendance — Lectures begin promptly at the start of the scheduled class period; arrive on time and stay for the full period. Regular attendance is one of the most important contributors to student success. If you need to miss class, contact Dr. Sasaki as soon as possible to discuss how to stay on track.
Illness — Please don’t attend class if you’re ill. Communicate your absence as soon as possible. You’ll have an opportunity to make up missed assignments, but it’s your responsibility to keep pace with lecture material.
Engagement and participation — Expect in-class questions, group discussions, and activities meant to build critical thinking and understanding. Reaching the correct answer matters, but the process of getting there matters more. All students are expected to be respectful and engaged — asking questions, taking good notes, giving full effort in group work, and paying attention when others are sharing.
Cell phones and laptops — Fine for notes or in-class activities; please avoid non-course use or distracting others. Persistent misuse may result in being asked to leave. Recording lectures without prior consent or a registered accommodation is not allowed.

Academic integrity policy
All students are advised of the university policy on academic integrity. Academic honesty is essential to maintaining trust in the learning environment and ensuring all students are evaluated fairly. Students are responsible for the honest completion and representation of their own work; academic dishonesty in any form (plagiarism, cheating, fabrication, facilitating dishonesty) will not be tolerated and may result in disciplinary action, up to and including failure of the assignment or course, and referral to the provost’s office.






AI statement



You are strongly discouraged from the use of AI and LLM agents (e.g., ChatGPT, Claude, etc.) in this course. While some uses — like proofreading written assignments or brainstorming ideas — can be beneficial, an increasingly common observation is that use of AI tools when learning new techniques (and especially when learning to code) blocks the development of skills and understanding.
Any AI usage must be documented in detail, and students must be able to describe how generated output was modified to reflect their own thoughts and perspective. Students are encouraged to think about (1) the consequences of AI usage for their own learning and for the environment, and (2) how AI use affects the development of critical thinking skills. As a general rule, assignments generated entirely or primarily by AI will not be accepted. In the event of suspected AI-generated responses, Dr. Sasaki may choose to check student understanding via a conversation and discuss how the answer was arrived at. After an initial warning, however, violations of this policy will be considered academic misconduct, subject to the university’s Academic Integrity procedures.

title: Syllabus
text:
Assignments
Over the course of the semester, you will complete a range of Assignments meant to develop your understanding of key points from the lecture materials. These assignments fall into three general categories:
Problem Sets – Students will complete weekly coding problem sets, questions about concepts and theory with application in both hypothetical and real-world scenarios. When analyzing example data sets, students will be asked to describe the methods and interpret results, as might be required when preparing scientific publications. Problem sets are graded on completion.
Data Safari Exercises – In these exercises, students are tasked to replicate a figure from the published literature using the publicly available data from that study. Students will also be asked to reflect on the process for each exercise: How easy was it to follow the published methods? How well does your plot match the published version? How would you change the paper, plot, or data to improve reproducibility?
Projects – In addition to the above components, graduate students are required to complete a project over the course of the semester. These projects will be broken down into the main analytic steps we will cover in this course – experimental design and planned hypothesis testing, data carpentry and exploration, statistical modelling, and visualization. Ideally, students will complete this project using their own data, but data obtained from the published literature is also acceptable. Projects will be presented at the end of the semester.
Assignments are distributed as Quarto (.qmd) templates, downloadable from the Schedule. Complete them in the template, then render to PDF (via Typst, bundled with Quarto) and submit both the .qmd and the .pdf. Given the pacing and breadth of this course, it is important to turn work in on time. Late assignments can be turned in for credit up to three weeks following the deadline, but will be docked 2% for every day past the due date (weekends included).

title: Week 14 Tutorial: When Assumptions Fail, and Choosing a Model
text:
A permutation test
Is the difference between spray C and spray A larger than expected by chance?

two <- InsectSprays |> filter(spray %in% c("A", "C")) |> droplevels()
obs <- coef(lm(count ~ spray, data = two))[2]

set.seed(14)
perm <- replicate(5000, {
  shuffled <- two
  shuffled$spray <- sample(shuffled$spray)
  coef(lm(count ~ spray, data = shuffled))[2]
})
mean(abs(perm) >= abs(obs))

[1] 0



ggplot(data.frame(perm), aes(perm)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 40) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = obs, linetype = "dashed") +
  theme_minimal()

text:

A hand-built 2×2 table: germination (yes/no) with and without cold stratification.

germ <- data.frame(

  germinated = rep(c("Yes", "No"), times = 2),

xtabs(n ~ treatment + germinated, germ)

            germinated
treatment    No Yes
  Control    22  18

title: Week 9 Tutorial: Everything Is a Linear Model
text:
One-sample and paired t-tests
The built-in sleep data: extra hours of sleep for 10 patients under two drugs. Each patient appears twice (this is a paired design).

sleep2 <- sleep |> rename(drug = group)
wide <- sleep2 |> pivot_wider(names_from = drug, values_from = extra, names_prefix = "drug")
wide$diff <- wide$drug2 - wide$drug1

The classic way:

t.test(wide$drug2, wide$drug1, paired = TRUE)


    Paired t-test

data:  wide$drug2 and wide$drug1
t = 4.0621, df = 9, p-value = 0.002833
alternative hypothesis: true mean difference is not equal to 0
95 percent confidence interval:
 0.7001142 2.4598858
sample estimates:
mean difference 
           1.58 


The linear model way: an intercept-only model on the differences.

m_paired <- lm(diff ~ 1, data = wide)
tidy(m_paired, conf.int = TRUE)

# A tibble: 1 x 7
  term        estimate std.error statistic p.value conf.low conf.high
  <chr>          <dbl>     <dbl>     <dbl>   <dbl>    <dbl>     <dbl>
1 (Intercept)     1.58     0.389      4.06 0.00283    0.700      2.46


Same t, same p, same confidence interval. The intercept is the mean difference.

title: Week 6 Tutorial: Design in Practice
section: A framework for reading a methods section
text:
A framework for reading a methods section
Whenever you read the methods of a paper, try to answer these questions, in this order:

What is the experimental unit? The thing that was independently assigned to a treatment — not necessarily the thing that was measured (recall Week 5’s pseudoreplication discussion).
What are the treatments/groups, and how many levels does each factor have?
How many experimental units per treatment (the replication)?
Was assignment to treatment randomized? If so, how — and if not, is it an observational study instead?
Was there any blocking, matching, or other control for a known source of variation?
What was the response variable, and how was it measured?
What statistical test or model did the authors use to analyze it — and does that choice match the design (matching what we covered in Weeks 5 and 7 onward)?

title: Week 6 Tutorial: Design in Practice
text:
Worked example (hypothetical)
Consider a hypothetical study: researchers want to know whether a soil amendment increases seedling survival in a restoration planting. They have 40 plots across a hillside, and randomly assign half to receive the amendment and half to serve as controls. Survival is recorded after one growing season.
Applying the framework:

Experimental unit: the plot (not the individual seedling — seedlings within a plot share soil and microclimate, so they aren’t independent).
Treatments: one factor, two levels (amendment vs. control).
Replication: 20 plots per treatment.
Randomization: yes — amendment assigned randomly across plots.
Blocking: none mentioned; if the hillside has a known elevation gradient, that’s a missed opportunity to block.
Response variable: proportion of seedlings surviving per plot.
Analysis: a logistic regression or a t-test on arcsine-transformed proportions would both be defensible choices here — this connects to Week 11’s lecture on the logistic alternative to lm().

text:
Simulating a randomized complete block design
Suppose greenhouse bench position affects plant growth independent of treatment. A randomized block design assigns each treatment once per bench (block), so bench-to-bench variation can be separated from treatment effects.

library(tidyverse)
set.seed(1)


n_blocks <- 6
treatments <- c("Control", "Low_N", "High_N")

design <- expand_grid(block = factor(1:n_blocks), treatment = treatments)

block_effect <- rnorm(n_blocks, mean = 0, sd = 3)
names(block_effect) <- levels(design$block)

design <- design |>
  mutate(
    trt_effect = case_when(
      treatment == "Control" ~ 0,
      treatment == "Low_N"   ~ 2,
      treatment == "High_N"  ~ 5
    ),
    growth = 20 + trt_effect + block_effect[as.character(block)] +
      rnorm(n(), 0, 1.5)
  )

A question to sit with

If you ran the same experiment twice, would you trust the second result as much as the first?

title: Why Experimental Design Matters

Why design comes before analysis

No statistical test can fix a poorly designed study
Common failure modes we’ll dissect this semester:

Pseudoreplication (measuring the same unit many times, treating it as many replicates)
Confounding (treatment tangled up with some other variable)
Underpowered studies (too few replicates to detect a real effect)

Why explore before modeling?

title: Principles of Experimental Design
text:
From exploring to designing

Weeks 1–4: get comfortable with R and with looking at data
Starting today: how do you make sure the data you collect can actually answer your question?

title: Principles of Experimental Design
text:
Three pillars

Replication — measuring enough independent experimental units
Randomization — assigning treatments in a way that avoids bias
Blocking — controlling for a known source of variation you’re not interested in

title: Principles of Experimental Design
text:
Replication: how many is enough?

More replicates → smaller standard errors → easier to detect a real effect
But replication means independent experimental units, not repeated measurements of the same unit
We’ll formalize “how many” with power analysis later in the course

title: Principles of Experimental Design
text:
The experimental unit, again

The thing that was independently assigned to a treatment
Not necessarily the thing you measured
Classic trap: 1 tank of 50 fish, “n = 50” — really n = 1 tank

title: Principles of Experimental Design
text:
Pseudoreplication

Treating non-independent measurements as if they were independent replicates
Inflates your effective sample size
Inflates your false-positive rate — you’ll find “significant” effects that aren’t real

title: Principles of Experimental Design
text:
Randomization

Protects against confounding: without it, treatment can get tangled up with some other variable (time of day, position, batch)
“I gave the healthiest-looking plants the new fertilizer” is not randomization — it’s a confound waiting to happen

title: Principles of Experimental Design
text:
Blocking

Groups experimental units into blocks that share some nuisance variable (bench position, day, litter, site)
Assign every treatment once within each block
Lets you statistically remove block-to-block variation from your error term

title: Principles of Experimental Design
text:
Blocking in action

Naive model: growth ~ treatment
Blocked model: growth ~ treatment + block
Blocking usually shrinks the residual variance, making it easier to detect the treatment effect — we’ll simulate this today

title: Principles of Experimental Design
text:
When blocking doesn’t help much

If the nuisance variable barely matters, blocking costs you degrees of freedom for little benefit
Worth checking, not assuming

text:

title: Design in Practice: Reading the Literature
text:
Why this matters

Textbook examples are clean by design
Real papers bury the design in a paragraph of prose — you have to extract it yourself
This is a skill you’ll use for the rest of your career, not just this course

title: Design in Practice: Reading the Literature
text:
A framework: seven questions

What is the experimental unit?
What are the treatments, and how many levels?
How many experimental units per treatment?
Was assignment randomized?
Was there blocking or matching?
What was the response variable, and how was it measured?
Does the statistical analysis match the design?

title: Design in Practice: Reading the Literature
text:
Question 1 is the hardest

Not “how many measurements” — “how many independently assigned units”
If you’re unsure, ask: what would it mean to have one more replicate here?

title: Design in Practice: Reading the Literature
text:
A worked example

Hypothetical: soil amendment vs. seedling survival, 40 plots, 20 per treatment, randomly assigned
Experimental unit: the plot (not the individual seedling)
Randomization: yes. Blocking: none — and the hillside likely has an elevation gradient that could have been blocked on

title: Design in Practice: Reading the Literature
text:
What “no blocking” costs you

Not necessarily wrong — just possibly less powerful than it could have been
Part of your job as a reader (and later, a designer) is spotting missed opportunities like this

title: Hypothesis Testing I: T-Tests and ANOVA
text:
The simplest case: two groups

Comparing a numeric outcome between exactly two groups
The tool: t.test()
Paired or unpaired? Depends on your design — measurements from the same subject under two conditions are paired

title: Hypothesis Testing I: T-Tests and ANOVA
text:
Three or more groups: ANOVA

Comparing means across 3+ groups
The tool: aov()
Null hypothesis: all group means are equal
A significant ANOVA tells you some group differs — not which

title: Hypothesis Testing I: T-Tests and ANOVA
text:
Checking assumptions

Residuals roughly normal (Q-Q plot)
Similar variance across groups (Levene’s test, residuals-vs-fitted plot)
These are exactly the checks Weeks 3–4 trained you to make

title: Hypothesis Testing I: T-Tests and ANOVA
section: After a significant ANOVA: post-hoc tests
text:
After a significant ANOVA: post-hoc tests

emmeans() + pairs() for pairwise comparisons
Correct for multiple comparisons (Tukey) — testing many pairs inflates your false-positive rate

title: Hypothesis Testing I: T-Tests and ANOVA
text:
From test back to design

A test only tells you what to do with data you already have
The design determines whether the data can answer your question at all
Example: 3 fertilizer doses, 1 greenhouse, 18 pots — what’s the experimental unit? How would you randomize?

title: Hypothesis Testing I: T-Tests and ANOVA
text:
A peek ahead

The t-test and ANOVA are special cases of the linear model: lm(y ~ group)
After Spring Break we’ll build everything else on that idea, and read models with the marginaleffects package

title: Everything Is a Linear Model
text:
Welcome back

Weeks 7 gave you a menu: t-test, ANOVA, …
The second half of the course replaces the menu with one idea:


Most common statistical tests are special cases of the linear model. — Jonas Lindeløv, Common statistical tests are linear models


Learn one framework deeply, and you can answer almost any question in this course

title: Everything Is a Linear Model
text:
The one equation
\[y = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_1 + \beta_2 x_2 + \dots + \varepsilon\]

In R: lm(y ~ 1 + x1 + x2)
The test you want is almost always a question about one or more β’s
Different tests = different choices of what goes on the right-hand side

title: Everything Is a Linear Model
text:
One sample and paired t-tests



Classic test
Linear model




One-sample t-test
lm(y ~ 1)


Paired t-test
lm(y2 - y1 ~ 1)




The intercept is the mean (or the mean difference)
The test of the intercept against 0 is the t-test

title: Everything Is a Linear Model
text:
Two groups and many groups



Classic test
Linear model




Two-sample t-test
lm(y ~ 1 + group)


One-way ANOVA
lm(y ~ 1 + group) + anova()




With a categorical predictor, R creates 0/1 dummy variables
Intercept = mean of the reference group; each slope = difference from it
t-test and ANOVA are the same model — two groups vs. three or more

title: Everything Is a Linear Model
text:
Continuous predictors



Classic test
Linear model




Pearson correlation
lm(y ~ 1 + x) (standardized)


Simple regression
lm(y ~ 1 + x)


Spearman correlation
lm(rank(y) ~ 1 + rank(x))




Slope = change in y per one-unit change in x
Correlation is just the slope when both variables are z-scored

title: Everything Is a Linear Model
text:
Why bother?

Fewer things to learn — and the assumptions are the same ones every time
Easy to extend — add a covariate, an interaction, a random effect
Better communication — an estimate with an interval, not just a p-value
Weeks 10–14 build directly on this: every new test is a small extension

title: Everything Is a Linear Model
section: A tool for reading models: marginaleffects
text:
A tool for reading models: marginaleffects

Model coefficients depend on how the model was coded (reference levels, interactions, link functions…)
marginaleffects asks questions in the units of the data:








Question
Function




What does the model predict?
predictions(), avg_predictions()


How does the outcome differ between groups / treatments?
comparisons(), avg_comparisons()


What’s the slope of the outcome in x?
slopes(), avg_slopes()


Custom tests of combinations
hypotheses()

title: Everything Is a Linear Model
section: The same three questions, every week
text:
The same three questions, every week

Fit a model (lm, glm, lmer, …)
Check its assumptions
Ask the question with marginaleffects


Same workflow Weeks 9–14, only the model in step 1 changes
Docs: marginaleffects.com

title: Everything Is a Linear Model
text:
Design still matters

A linear model can’t tell you whether the data can answer your question
Randomized treatment → causal estimate; measured predictor → association
The model describes; the design justifies

title: Multiple Regression, ANCOVA, and Interactions
text:
Last week

t-tests, ANOVA, and correlation are all lm() with one predictor
This week: more than one predictor — the models that biological experiments actually need




Classic test
Linear model




ANCOVA
lm(y ~ group + x)


Two-way ANOVA
lm(y ~ A * B)


Multiple regression
lm(y ~ x1 + x2)

title: Multiple Regression, ANCOVA, and Interactions
text:
Why add predictors?

Control for a nuisance variable (e.g., initial size) → less noise, more power
Ask about two factors at once (e.g., supplement and dose)
Ask whether an effect depends on context → interactions

title: Multiple Regression, ANCOVA, and Interactions
text:
ANCOVA

lm(y ~ group + x): group differences adjusted for a continuous covariate
Fits parallel lines, one per group
The group coefficient = vertical distance between the lines

title: Multiple Regression, ANCOVA, and Interactions
text:
Interactions

y ~ group * x means y ~ group + x + group:x
The lines can now have different slopes
“Does the effect of x depend on group?” is a question about the group:x term

title: Multiple Regression, ANCOVA, and Interactions
text:
The interaction problem

With an interaction, “the effect of group” has no single value — it depends on x
Raw coefficients become hard to read: reference levels, centered or not…
This is where reading the table of coefficients stops working

title: Multiple Regression, ANCOVA, and Interactions
text:
Marginal effects to the rescue
marginaleffects answers questions in the units of the data:

avg_slopes(m, variables = "x", by = "group") — the slope of x within each group
avg_comparisons(m, variables = "group", by = "dose") — the group effect at each dose
plot_predictions(m, condition = c("x", "group")) — the picture

title: Multiple Regression, ANCOVA, and Interactions
text:
Marginal means vs. marginal effects

Predictions — the model’s expected outcome at chosen values (predictions(), avg_predictions())
Comparisons — differences or ratios of predictions (comparisons())
Slopes — the rate of change (slopes())
Averaged (“avg_”) over the sample, or evaluated at datagrid() values you choose

title: Multiple Regression, ANCOVA, and Interactions
text:
Effect sizes

A p-value says whether an effect is detectable; an estimate with an interval says how big
Marginal effects are effect sizes in the original units (grams, mm, seconds)
Report: estimate, 95% CI, and what it means biologically

title: Multiple Regression, ANCOVA, and Interactions
text:
Collinearity and caution

Correlated predictors → unstable coefficients (check VIF, performance::check_collinearity())
Interpretation of a coefficient is always “holding the others constant”
Adding predictors doesn’t fix a flawed design

title: Generalized Linear Models
section: When the response isn’t a nice bell curve
text:
When the response isn’t a nice bell curve

Survived / died. Germinated / didn’t. Number of insects.
A straight-line model can predict impossible values (negative counts, probabilities over 1)
Fix: keep the linear model, but model a transformation of the mean

title: Generalized Linear Models
text:
The generalized linear model
\[g(\text{mean of } y) = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_1 + \dots\]

The right-hand side is still the linear model you know
g() is the link function; the family says what the noise looks like




Response
Family
Link




Continuous
gaussian
identity (= lm)


Binary (0/1)
binomial
logit


Counts
poisson
log

title: Generalized Linear Models
text:
Logistic regression

glm(survived ~ shade, family = binomial)
Coefficients are log-odds — hard to think in!
exp(coef) gives odds ratios — still hard

title: Generalized Linear Models
text:
Marginal effects make GLMs readable

avg_predictions(m) — predicted probabilities
avg_comparisons(m) — the difference in probability between conditions (risk difference)
comparison = "ratio" — risk ratio; "lnor" — log odds ratio
Same function calls as Weeks 9–10, now on the response scale

title: Generalized Linear Models
text:
Count data

glm(count ~ treatment, family = poisson)
Coefficients are log rate ratios
Watch for overdispersion: variance bigger than the mean → quasipoisson or negative binomial

title: Generalized Linear Models
section: Chi-square tests are linear models too
text:
Chi-square tests are linear models too



Classic test
Model




Goodness of fit
glm(n ~ 1, poisson)


Chi-square test of independence
glm(n ~ row * col, poisson)




Cell counts are the response; the interaction is the test of association
Same result as chisq.test(), but now you can add predictors

title: Generalized Linear Models
text:
Design reminder

Binary outcomes need larger samples than continuous ones
Beware complete separation: a predictor that perfectly predicts the outcome
Replication unit still matters: 100 seeds in 1 dish is n = 1 for dish effects

title: Non-Independence: Mixed-Effects Models I
section: A problem we’ve flagged since Week 5
text:
A problem we’ve flagged since Week 5

Pseudoreplication: measurements from the same site, subject, or plot aren’t independent
Ignoring this inflates your effective sample size and false-positive rate
Today: a proper tool for handling it, instead of just avoiding it

title: Non-Independence: Mixed-Effects Models I
text:
You’ve already seen it

The paired t-test handles non-independence: each patient measured twice
In Week 9: lm(y2 - y1 ~ 1)
Another way: keep both measurements, and give each subject its own intercept

title: Non-Independence: Mixed-Effects Models I
text:
Random intercepts
\[y_{ij} = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_{ij} + u_j + \varepsilon_{ij}, \quad u_j \sim N(0, \sigma_u^2)\]

Each group j (subject, site, chick) has its own baseline \(u_j\)
One shared effect \(\beta_1\) is estimated for everyone
lmer(y ~ x + (1 | subject))

title: Non-Independence: Mixed-Effects Models I
text:
Fixed vs. random effects

Fixed: levels you care about (treatment, diet)
Random: groups sampled from a larger population (site, subject, tank)
Random effects estimate a variance, not one coefficient per level

title: Non-Independence: Mixed-Effects Models I
text:
Paired t-test = random-intercept model



Classic test
Linear model




Paired t-test
lm(y2 - y1 ~ 1)


Paired t-test (long data)
lmer(y ~ condition + (1 \| subject))




Same estimate, same t, same p
But the mixed model generalizes: unbalanced data, more than two time points, covariates

title: Non-Independence: Mixed-Effects Models I
text:
Population vs. subject-specific predictions

With random effects, “the prediction” is ambiguous:

for a typical subject (random effects set to zero)?
for a specific subject?

In marginaleffects: re.form = NA gives population-level predictions
Marginal effects of the fixed effects are on the same scale as before

title: Non-Independence: Mixed-Effects Models I
text:
Reading a mixed model

avg_comparisons() for the treatment contrast
avg_slopes(..., by = "diet") for slopes within groups
plot_predictions(m, condition = "Time", re.form = NA) for the population trend
The variance of the random effect tells you how much groups differ at baseline (VarCorr())

title: Non-Independence: Mixed-Effects Models I
text:
Design reminder

A mixed model fixes the statistics, not the design
You still need enough groups (≥5–6 for each random effect)
Replication happens at the level where treatment is applied

title: Mixed-Effects Models II
text:
Last week

Random intercepts: each group has its own baseline
But groups often differ in how they respond too

title: Mixed-Effects Models II
text:
Random slopes

lmer(y ~ x + (1 + x | subject))
Each subject gets their own intercept and their own slope
The fixed effect is the average slope; the random effect is how much it varies

title: Mixed-Effects Models II
text:
Why random slopes matter

If the effect truly varies across groups and you leave out the random slope, standard errors are too small
Keep it maximal where design supports it: random slopes for effects that vary within groups
If the model won’t converge, simplify (and report it)

title: Mixed-Effects Models II
text:
Nested vs. crossed

Nested: each lower unit belongs to exactly one higher unit (cask within batch)

(1 | batch/cask)

Crossed: every unit appears in several higher units (every sample on every plate)

(1 | plate) + (1 | sample)

Draw your design — the structure comes from the design, not from the data

title: Mixed-Effects Models II
text:
Marginal effects in mixed models

Fixed-effect marginal effects: same avg_slopes() / avg_comparisons()
Population-level: re.form = NA
Subject-specific predictions are possible too, via newdata
Report the variance components alongside the fixed effects

Today: what to do when the assumptions don’t hold, and how to pick a model for a new problem

title: When Assumptions Fail, and Choosing a Model
section: “Nonparametric” tests are linear models on ranks
text:
“Nonparametric” tests are linear models on ranks



Classic test
Linear model




Spearman correlation
lm(rank(y) ~ 1 + rank(x))


Mann-Whitney U
lm(signed_rank(y) ~ 1 + group)


Kruskal-Wallis
lm(rank(y) ~ group)


Wilcoxon signed-rank
lm(signed_rank(y) ~ 1)




Replace values by ranks, then run the same model
Close approximations (not exact) for larger samples

title: When Assumptions Fail, and Choosing a Model
text:
The cost of ranks

You lose the original units: “the rank difference is 7.2” isn’t an effect size
Hard to extend to covariates and random effects
Prefer transforms, GLMs, or robust standard errors when you can

title: When Assumptions Fail, and Choosing a Model
text:
Better options for violated assumptions



Problem
Fix




Unequal variances
Robust standard errors (vcov = "HC3")


Skewed response
Transform, or use a GLM


Counts or proportions
glm() with the right family


Non-independence
Mixed model


Tiny samples, odd statistics
Permutation / bootstrap

title: When Assumptions Fail, and Choosing a Model
text:
Robust standard errors with marginaleffects

Welch’s t-test and friends are about unequal variance
avg_comparisons(m, variables = "group", vcov = "HC3")
Same estimate, honest uncertainty

title: When Assumptions Fail, and Choosing a Model
text:
Permutation tests

Idea: if treatment did nothing, labels are exchangeable
Shuffle labels, refit, repeat; compare observed statistic to the shuffled distribution
Works for any statistic you can compute from a model

title: When Assumptions Fail, and Choosing a Model
text:
Choosing a model

What is the response? continuous → lm; binary → binomial; count → poisson
What are the predictors? groups, covariates, interactions
Is the data independent? if not → random effects
What question am I asking? → avg_comparisons, avg_slopes, hypotheses

title: When Assumptions Fail, and Choosing a Model
text:
The course in one slide

A statistical test is a model + a question about its parameters
The model comes from the design: responses, predictors, structure
The question is answered with marginal effects in the units of the data
Check assumptions, report estimates with intervals
